standard.title: Interpret observations and comparisons
standard.description: interpret information and data from observations and provided sources, including the comparison of objects from the past and present
standard.prior_knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFS02, AC9HSFS03): Students sorted information from sources and shared perspectives. From AC9HS1S02: Students collected and recorded information from observations and sources.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students interpret information from observations and provided sources, including comparing objects from the past and present.

nodes.label: Using sources to answer questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use information from sources (stories, photographs, satellite images, rock art, fieldwork observations) to answer 'when', 'where', 'what', 'how' and 'why' questions.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one source to answer at least two different types of questions (e.g. a 'what' and a 'where' question).
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of sources to answer When, Where, What, How and Why questions; identify what each source tells them and what it does not tell them; explore First Nations Australian stories about places and the past.
wider: Compare what traditional and contemporary First Nations Australian stories reveal about how places have changed
Use multiple sources on the same topic and identify where they agree and where they provide different information
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot extract targeted answers from sources, they cannot compare past and present objects — the comparison in Node 2 requires first being able to read what sources actually say.

response_modes.reason: Model source-reading explicitly: 'What does this photograph tell me? What question does it answer?' Use think-alouds before expecting students to do this independently.

success_criteria: Uses at least one source to answer at least two types of questions
Explains what the source tells them rather than inferring unsupported information

nodes.label: Comparing past and present objects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare objects or artefacts from the past with those used today, identifying similarities and differences using comparative language.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two objects from the past and present (e.g. old and new toys, phones, cooking tools) identifying one similarity and one difference.
nodes.typical_width: Compare a range of objects from the past with current equivalents (toys, games, clothes, phones, cooking utensils, tools, homework books); categorise similarities and differences; use comparative language accurately.
wider: Arrange a sequence of three or more versions of the same object over time and describe the trajectory of change
Categorise observed changes by type (material, purpose, size, technology) and discuss which types of change are most common

response_modes.reason: More objects compared means more robust understanding of change patterns — build range of comparison objects across multiple categories.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing across multiple categories of objects (technology, clothing, food, play) reveals different rates and patterns of change — this creates genuinely richer historical thinking than comparing within one category only.
success_criteria: Compares at least two objects from different time periods
Identifies at least one similarity and one difference using comparative language

nodes.label: Categorising features of places
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can categorise objects, drawings or images by their features and explain the reason for their categorisation, applying this to place features (natural, constructed, managed).
nodes.minimum_width: Categorise at least six items into natural, constructed and managed categories and explain one reason for each category assignment.
nodes.typical_width: Categorise features of local places into natural, constructed and managed types; explain reasons for categorisation; compare categorisations with peers and resolve disagreements.
wider: Categorise the same feature differently from multiple perspectives and discuss how viewpoint affects categorisation
Apply the three categories to a place that has changed over time and identify whether the change shifted its category

response_modes.reason: Categorisation with reasoning integrates source interpretation and place classification — the explanatory demand ('explain the reason') is the integration test.

success_criteria: Categorises features of a local place into natural, constructed and managed types
Explains the reason for at least one categorisation decision
